teach.title: The subject on the receiving end
teach.say: When the subject is not doing but being done to, the verb takes a second set of endings: **the passive person endings (I am …-ed, you are …-ed …)**. *Discipulus ā magistrō pūnītur* — the pupil is punished by the teacher. Nothing is added in front of the verb, as English adds *am, are, is*; the ending alone carries it.

check.ask: laudor and laudāris: which one is 'I am praised'?

teach.title: The singular: -or, -ris, -tur
teach.say: *-or* I am …-ed, *-ris* you are …-ed, *-tur* he or she is …-ed: *laudor, laudāris, laudātur*. Set them beside the active *-ō, -s, -t* and each one is simply that ending with an *r* in it. The *r* is what your eye should catch.

check.ask: Fill the three singular passive cells of laudāre: I am praised, you are, he is.

teach.title: The plural: -mur, -minī, -ntur
teach.say: *-mur* we are …-ed, *-minī* you all are …-ed, *-ntur* they are …-ed: *laudāmur, laudāminī, laudantur*. *-minī* is the odd one, the only ending in the set without an *r*, so it is worth learning on its own.

check.ask: Fill the three plural passive cells of laudāre: we are praised, you all are, they are.

teach.title: Who did it: ā or ab with the ablative
teach.say: The passive can name the doer, and does it with *ā* (or *ab* in front of a vowel) and the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form): *ā magistrō laudātur*, he is praised by the teacher. With no such phrase the sentence simply does not say who did it — which is often exactly why the passive was chosen.

check.ask: portātur: what person, number and voice is it, and which two words add the doer?

teach.title: The vowel in front still belongs to the verb
teach.say: The six endings never change; the vowel before them does: *laudā-tur*, *vidē-tur*, *leg-i-tur*, *audī-tur*. One cell is worth marking: in the third conjugation (the -ere family) 'you are …-ed' is *legeris*, with an *e* where the other forms have *i*.

check.ask: legitur: what person, number and voice, and what is the vowel before the ending doing?

teach.title: The same endings serve a deponent
teach.say: *sequitur* wears these very endings and means 'he follows', because it is **a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks)**. Two tests keep them apart: a deponent may carry an object in the accusative (the object form), and it never names a doer with *ā* or *ab*, since nothing is being done to it.

check.ask: sequitur and vidētur end alike. Which one is the sailor's own doing?

core.text: The passive has its own six endings: **the passive person endings (I am …-ed, you are …-ed …)**. *-or* I am, *-ris* you are, *-tur* he is, *-mur* we are, *-minī* you all are, *-ntur* they are. *Ego ā magistrō laudor* — I am praised by the teacher; *tū laudāris, nōs laudāmur, vōs laudāminī*. Each matches an active ending: *-ō → -or, -s → -ris, -t → -tur, -mus → -mur, -tis → -minī, -nt → -ntur*. The same set serves a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks): *sequor, sequeris, sequitur, sequimur, sequiminī, sequuntur*. Latin name: dēsinentiae persōnālēs passīvae.
Passive means the subject receives the action: *I am praised*, not *I praise*. English needs *am / are / is* plus *-ed*; Latin folds it into the ending.
-or, -ris, -tur, -mur, -minī, -ntur — the r-endings; -minī is the odd one out.

invented.en: We are loved by our father.

core.text: Active and passive differ only in the ending: *laudās* — you praise; *laudāris* — you are praised. One look-alike: 3rd-conjugation *-eris* is present passive (*mergeris*), while the future has long *-ēris*. Read the *r*: it marks the passive, or a deponent.

more.text: The 3rd conjugation shows *-eris, -imur, -iminī, -untur*. The 1st-conjugation *a* drops before *-or* just as before *-ō*: *iactō / iactor*. In the imperfect and in the subjunctive the first person ends in *-r* instead of *-or*: *laudābar* (I was being praised), *lauder*, *laudārer*. The future keeps *-or* in the 1st and 2nd conjugations (*laudābor* — I shall be praised) and has *-ar* in the 3rd and 4th (*mittar*). The agent goes with *ā / ab* + ablative: *ā magistrō laudor*.

The learner's notes (week 17): the passive / deponent endings are *-or / -r, -(e)ris, -(i)tur, -(i)mur, -(i)minī, -(u)ntur*, with the variable vowels working as in the active (*frang-eris, frang-imur, frang-iminī*); *-r* is the alternative to *-or* just as *-m* is to *-ō*, and is not used in the present indicative; the *a* of *a-*stems drops in the first person singular (*oper-or*) — with the active *-ō*, the only place in the whole verb system where a fixed stem vowel is lost.

Ørberg (chapter XVII): *laudor laudāmur, videor vidēmur, mergor mergimur, audior audīmur*; the deponents *laetor, vereor, sequor, partior* follow the same four patterns; *-iō* verbs go *capior, capiuntur* and *ēgredior, ēgrediuntur*; *ā magistrō laudor = magister mē laudat*.
